slides.q: How a spectrofluorometer records excitation and emission spectra

items.title: Fluorometer schematic
items.cap: Animated schematic of the Fluorolog-3 light path; spectrum shapes are sketches of sfGFP’s known spectra

points.text: Question: now that we have purified chimeras, does adding the tet groups, or the mechanical tension of the DNA spring, change sfGFP’s fluorescence?

Instrument: HORIBA Jobin Yvon Fluorolog-3. Xe lamp → excitation monochromator (picks the colour that hits the sample) → cuvette → emission monochromator at 90° (picks the colour counted) → detector S1; a reference photodiode R1 tracks the lamp
Excitation spectrum: hold the detected wavelength at 510 nm and sweep the excitation 400→500 nm. It shows which colours the chromophore absorbs and turns into fluorescence
Emission spectrum: hold the excitation at 485 nm and sweep the detected wavelength 500→600 nm. It shows what colour, and how much, light comes out
485 nm and 510 nm are sfGFP’s known excitation and emission maxima. The small 400 nm band is the neutral chromophore: it is the basis of our band ratio

slides.title: Effect of Tet quenching - tet addition dims excitation peak

callouts.html: Band ratio = I(400) / I(peak) on the lamp-corrected excitation spectrum: concentration-independent up to 8 µM (concentration-series slide), and every reading here is ≤ 10 µM. Concentrations under each bar, in chronological order. * Attempt 1 is only an estimate: we had no accurate BCA or NanoDrop readings yet and trusted a 40 µM stock that turned out to be mislabelled.

slides.title: Concentration ladder - inner filter effect

callouts.html: What justifies the use of band ratio as our fluorometry metric?

Why this metric? Concentration independence: I(400) and I(peak) both scale with the amount of protein, so their ratio cancels it and reports only the chromophore’s neutral/anionic balance. That holds only below the inner filter effect (the sample absorbs the excitation light before it reaches the detected volume; literature: from ≈ 5 µM). Here the ratio is flat up to 8 µM and rises from 16 µM; every reading we compare is ≤ 10 µM.

slides.title: What the band ratio measures
slides.q: Interactive: 1-tet concentration series, 2026-08-25

items.cap: Lamp-corrected excitation spectra, normalised to peak = 1 (mean of n = 3 per concentration)

points.text: Purpose: a concentration-independent readout. Both intensities scale with the amount of protein, so their ratio cancels it and tracks only the chromophore’s neutral/anionic balance
Band ratio = I(400) / I(peak), read off each sample’s lamp-corrected excitation spectrum (S1 ÷ R1)
I(peak): the spectrum’s maximum, ≈ 485–489 nm, the anionic chromophore band
I(400): the intensity at 400 nm, the neutral chromophore band
With peak = 1, each curve’s height at 400 nm is its band ratio: 2–4 µM lowest (≈ 0.10), 32 µM highest (0.146)
Dividing by I(peak) cancels concentration and lamp drift, but only at low absorbance: from 16 µM the inner filter effect lifts the ratio; all our comparisons are at ≤ 10 µM
Try it: click legend entries to hide traces, drag across the plot to zoom, double-click to reset

slides.title: What is MD analysis? How?
sfGFP MD: the protein and the simulated systems

items.cap: Structure: what each part is
Overview: barrel, two Tet2-Et/sTCO tethers, 27 bp duplex
Strain: putty tube scaled by per-residue RMSF
Chromophore: the three H-bonds that stop it twisting

explain.text: sfGFP architecture (238 residues). β-strands: extended segments hydrogen-bonded side by side; eleven of them form the β-barrel wall (≈ 42 Å tall, 24 Å across), the rigid part. A central α-helix threads the barrel axis and carries the chromophore (made from Thr65–Tyr66–Gly67), sealed off from solvent; short helices also sit on the caps. Loops: the short, irregular segments that join one strand to the next at the two ends (caps) of the barrel. Nothing holds them in the sheet, so they are the most mobile parts (e.g. residues 189–194 between strands 9 and 10).

The spring. Our tethers (orange, Tet2-Et clicked to sTCO) attach at Asp133 and Asn149 (red), 31.3 Å apart across the barrel, with His148, which bonds the chromophore, between them. The DNA spring (blue) spans the two tethers and pushes or pulls on the sites.

points.text: Sites: Asp133 and Asn149, 31.3 Å apart, with His148 between them bonded to the chromophore
Systems compared: WT sfGFP · tethers unclicked vs clicked (no DNA, the zero) · DNA springs of various lengths · dsDNA vs ssDNA · intact vs nicked duplex · a direct force clamp
Animations show the 27 bp spring chimera (50 ns, water stripped, superposed on the barrel core)
Scale: 4,050 ns of production, 81 replicates across 17 systems

items.cap: Backbone φ/ψ at the two modified sites

explain.text: <dfn>Ramachandran plot</dfn>: every dot is one simulation frame, placed by the two backbone dihedral angles of a single residue. <dfn>φ (phi)</dfn>, x-axis: rotation about the N–Cα bond. <dfn>ψ (psi)</dfn>, y-axis: rotation about the Cα–C bond. Both run −180° to +180°. The boxes are the allowed regions: β / PPII (extended strand), right-handed α (helix) and left-handed α (rare; mostly Gly, Asp, Asn). Large symbols are each system’s mean. If a modification strains the backbone, its cloud leaves the WT basin.

Left panel: site 133 (Asp133). Right panel: site 149 (Asn149). Colours: blue wild type, orange 2× Tet2-Et unclicked, green clicked adduct. The two sites sit on adjacent β-strands with His148, which bonds the chromophore, between them.

points.text: Asp133 sits in the rare left-handed α basin: WT +57, +16
Unclicked 2× Tet2-Et pushes it to +74, +2, about 17.5° out of the basin
After the click it returns to +60, +18, back beside WT
Answer: no significant change; only a local, reversible shift at the one positive-φ site

slides.title: sfGFP: backbone rigidity (RMSF)
slides.q: Is the backbone rigid, with and without force?

items.cap: Cα RMSF, aligned on the barrel core
Axial force clamp on the unclicked protein

explain.text: RMSF (root-mean-square fluctuation): how far each residue’s Cα atom wanders from its own average position over the trajectory, after every frame is aligned on the rigid core. Low = rigid, high = mobile. x-axis: residue number (2B3P numbering); y-axis: Cα RMSF (Å). Dashed lines mark the chromophore (CRO 66) and the attachment sites Asp133, His148, Asn149. One colour per system. The low, flat stretches (≈ 0.4 Å) are the β-strands of the barrel wall. The peaks are loops, the short connectors between strands at the barrel caps: the tallest is residues 189–194 (between strands 9 and 10, ≈ 1.5 Å), then 155–158 and 211–212.

<dfn>Axial force clamp</dfn>: a constant force F applied directly between the Cβ atoms of Asp133 and Asn149 of the unclicked protein, pulling them apart, with no DNA: a controlled stand-in for a spring. x-axis: F (pN); y-axis: Cβ–Cβ distance (Å), mean ± sem of 3 replicates. Shaded: ±0.5 Å around the unloaded (0 pN) distance.

points.text: The β-barrel stays uniformly rigid (≈ 0.4 Å on the strands) in every system, including WT with no force at all
RMSF traces overlie each other; only the loops and the tethers move
With no force, the site distance is 31.61 ± 0.07 Å: the unloaded barrel barely fluctuates
0 → 20 pN shifts it by only 0.14 Å; the 4 pN dip is replicate noise. Compliance 0.0105 ± 0.0057 Å/pN (includes zero), so κ > 107 kBT nm⁻²
Answer: the backbone is already super rigid without any force, and force barely changes it

slides.title: sfGFP: forces applied, force field vs model
slides.q: How hard does a bent duplex push in the force field?

items.cap: Force measured on the bare duplex, one point per run

explain.text: The experiment. A bare duplex (the double-stranded DNA alone: 27 bp, 40 bp or 40 bp nicked; no protein) is held by a harmonic restraint on its end-to-end separation r, the distance between the two linker nitrogens that would attach to the protein:U(r) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,k\,(r - x_0)^2, \qquad F = k\,(\langle r\rangle - x_0)r: the end-to-end separation in each frame; x_0: the separation the restraint is centred on (one per run); k: restraint stiffness, 200 (stiff) or 33 (soft) kJ mol⁻¹ nm⁻². The duplex wants to straighten, so it sits at \langle r\rangle > x_0; the restraint then holds it with exactly the force F that the duplex pushes with.

Reading the plot. x-axis: \langle r\rangle, where the duplex actually sat (Å); y-axis: F (pN). Every point is one run. Colour = duplex (blue 27 bp, red 40 bp, green 40 bp nicked); shape = restraint (circle stiff, square soft). Solid lines: mean force per duplex. Dashed: the Euler buckling load F_E = \pi^2 B / L^2 (B = 200 pN nm², L = contour length), the push of a smoothly bent elastic rod. Grey band: what Zocchi’s kinked branch predicts for the same duplexes.

points.text: Measured: 27 bp 28.0 ± 1.2 pN (25 runs), 40 bp 15.8 ± 1.6 pN (10 runs), 40 bp nicked 13.2 pN
Roughly flat across ⟨r⟩: the duplex pushes with about the same force however far its ends are pushed together, as a buckled rod does
Close to the Euler load (dashed: 26.8 pN for 27 bp, 11.9 pN for 40 bp)
Zocchi’s kinked branch (grey) predicts only 2.4–6.6 pN: 5–6× less
What we learn: the force-field duplex behaves as a smoothly bent, unkinked rod pushing tens of pN. The next two slides show why Zocchi’s model expects less

slides.title: sfGFP: DNA dynamics
slides.q: Is the DNA kinked or coiled? Does it interact with the protein beyond pushing?

items.cap: Axis bend per base-pair step along each duplex

explain.text: x-axis: base pair along the duplex in the chimera; y-axis: <dfn>axis bend</dfn> at that base-pair step (°), the angle between the local helix axes either side of it. Line: mean across replicates; band: ± sd. A <dfn>kink</dfn> is a sharp local break of the duplex: it would show as one narrow spike. Smooth bending spreads the angle evenly.

points.text: The duplex bends smoothly at 4.8–5.2°/bp, nucleosome-like, with no local spike
The highest single step stays a broad bump, not a kink
The DNA touches the protein in 72–98 % of frames (ssDNA loop 93 %): local contact, not action at a distance
Answer: no kink, no coiling of the duplex; but the DNA lies against the protein

slides.title: sfGFP: Zocchi’s DNA-spring model, kinked and unkinked
slides.q: What does Zocchi’s model (Molecular Machines §2.15) predict for our springs?

points.text: Setup. A duplex of N base pairs is an elastic rod with contour length L = 0.33\,\mathrm{nm}\times N and bending modulus B = k_BT\,\ell_p \approx 200\ \mathrm{pN\,nm^2} (persistence length ℓp ≈ 50 nm, kBT = 4.1 pN nm). Its ends are held at end-to-end distance x < L, so it must bend, and it pushes them apart with a force f(x).

Unkinked branch (smoothly bent rod), eq. 2.203: the first term is the elastic push of the bent rod, the second a correction for its thermal fluctuationsf_{\mathrm{unkinked}}(x) = \frac{10\,B}{L^2} - \frac{k_BT}{L - x}

Kinked branch: the rod breaks at one point, with kink energy E_k = \tau_c \arccos(x/2R) (eq. 2.196); the force is f = -\,dE_k/dx:f_{\mathrm{kinked}}(x) = \frac{\tau_c}{2R\sqrt{1-(x/2R)^2}}, \qquad R = \frac{L}{2}\Big(1-\frac{\gamma^2}{90}\Big)

Which branch? The rod kinks once its bending torque reaches the critical torque τc ≈ 27 (nicked) to 34 (intact) pN nm, i.e. when x drops below (eqs 2.188, 2.194)x_c = L\Big(1-\frac{\gamma^2}{15}\Big), \qquad \gamma = \frac{L\,\tau_c}{2B}

Our springs. 27 bp: L = 8.9 nm, γ = 0.76, xc = 86 Å. The sfGFP chimeras span 63–73 Å < xc, so the model puts them on the kinked branch: f ≈ 5.5–6.8 pN (40 bp: xc = 121 Å, f ≈ 3.0 pN). In curvature terms, kinking starts at τc/B = 2.6–3.2°/bp, and our chimeras are bent 4.8–5.2°/bp
But the simulated duplexes never kinked (smooth bending, previous slide). So the force field should be compared with the unkinked branch: next slide

slides.title: sfGFP: the unkinked branch is the Euler load, and matches the force field
slides.q: Showing that the force-field measurement sits on Zocchi’s unkinked branch

points.text: 1 · Euler buckling. A rod of length L under end load F bends with shape y(s):B\,y''(s) + F\,y(s) = 0,\quad y(0)=y(L)=0 \;\Rightarrow\; y = A\sin\frac{\pi s}{L},\quad F_E = \frac{\pi^2 B}{L^2}Once buckled, it pushes back with ≈ FE almost regardless of how far its ends are pushed together

2 · The unkinked branch is the Euler load. Split Zocchi’s formula:f_{\mathrm{unkinked}}(x) = \underbrace{\frac{\pi^2 B}{L^2}}_{F_E} + \underbrace{\frac{(10-\pi^2)\,B}{L^2}}_{+1.3\%\ \text{of}\ F_E} - \underbrace{\frac{k_BT}{L-x}}_{\text{thermal}}27 bp at the measured ⟨x⟩ = 4.9 nm: FE = 24.9, +0.3, −1.0 pN, so funkinked = 24.2 pN, within 3 % of FE (40 bp: 10.9 vs 11.3 pN)

3 · The force field (previous slides):\langle F\rangle_{\mathrm{FF}} = k\,(\langle r\rangle - x_0) = 28.0 \pm 1.2\ \mathrm{pN}\ (27\ \mathrm{bp}),\quad 15.8 \pm 1.6\ \mathrm{pN}\ (40\ \mathrm{bp})flat across ⟨r⟩, the buckled-rod signature of step 1

4 · Set them equal. If the force-field duplex is an unkinked rod, \langle F\rangle_{\mathrm{FF}} = \pi^2 B_{\mathrm{FF}}/L^2, soB_{\mathrm{FF}} = \frac{\langle F\rangle_{\mathrm{FF}}\,L^2}{\pi^2}, \qquad \ell_p^{\mathrm{FF}} = \frac{B_{\mathrm{FF}}}{k_BT}27 bp: BFF = 209–225 pN nm², ℓp = 51–55 nm; 40 bp: 265–279 pN nm², 64–68 nm (range: L counted over N or N − 1 base-pair steps). Real DNA: ℓp ≈ 50 nm. The measurement is the unkinked branch with ordinary DNA stiffness
5 · The kinked branch cannot fit. At the same ⟨x⟩ it gives 4.6 pN (27 bp) and 3.0 pN (40 bp), 6× and 5× below the measurement

Conclusion: the force field and Zocchi agree on the unkinked spring (F ≈ π²B/L²). They differ only on whether the duplex kinks at 4.8–5.2°/bp: Zocchi’s τc = 27–34 pN nm says it should, the force-field duplex does not

slides.title: sfGFP: why fluorometry saw no change across ss, ds and nicked
slides.q: Excitation/emission wavelengths and band ratio barely moved. Does the MD explain it?

items.cap: Chromophore (green) inside the barrel with the 27 bp spring attached; dashed: its three key H-bonds
Occupancy of each chromophore H-bond, per system (ticks = replicates, filled = mean)

explain.text: What sets the colour and brightness. The chromophore (CRO 66) is buried in the β-barrel and held flat by a hydrogen-bond network: Thr203 and His148 to the phenolate oxygen, Arg96 and Gln94 to the imidazolinone carbonyl. Its excitation/emission wavelengths depend on this electrostatic environment and its protonation state; its brightness drops if it can twist about the two bonds of the methine bridge (a free chromophore is essentially dark). His148 sits between the two attachment sites, the mechanical path from the spring to the fluorophore.

Each row is one hydrogen bond around the chromophore; x-axis: <dfn>occupancy</dfn>, the % of frames in which the bond is formed (H···acceptor < 2.5 Å and angle > 120°). Ticks are individual replicates, filled symbols the means; one colour per system (WT, 2× Tet2-Et, clicked no DNA, 27 / 40 / 40-nicked bp springs). If a spring were prising the barrel open near the chromophore, the load-bearing bonds would fall.

points.text: Load-bearing bonds hold in every system: Arg96 100 %, Thr203 96–97 %, Gln94 92–97 %
His148 → phenolate: 72 % (WT) vs 72–82 % with springs, inside its own 39–92 % replicate scatter
Chromophore planarity unchanged: bridge twists τ 5.1–5.6°, φ 6.0–6.5° in all systems; cavity water 9–11 molecules
The barrel is stiff: RMSF ≈ 0.4 Å on the strands, κ > 107 k<sub>B</sub>T nm⁻² (0 → 20 pN moves the sites 0.14 Å, slide 15)
Answer: the springs never deform the chromophore’s environment, so no wavelength shift or band-ratio change is expected; seeing one would need a softer site or far stronger force

items.cap: Cα RMSF aligned on the core, HEAT repeats shaded
Bend and twist per HEAT repeat; horseshoe aperture

explain.text: <dfn>RMSF</dfn> (root-mean-square fluctuation): how far each residue’s Cα atom wanders from its own average position over the trajectory, after every frame is aligned on the rigid core. Low = rigid, high = mobile. x-axis: residue (UniProt numbering), HEAT repeats 1–15 shaded and numbered along the top; y-axis: Cα RMSF (Å), aligned on the core (residues 14–589). Dashed lines: the attachment sites Asp7 and Asn553. Apo, unclicked, clicked and 50 nt ssDNA are drawn; the 50 bp dsDNA run is off this scale.

Left: <dfn>bend</dfn> at each HEAT repeat, the angle between the solenoid axis entering and leaving it (°). Middle: <dfn>superhelical twist</dfn> per step (°). Right: the horseshoe <dfn>aperture</dfn>, the HEAT1–HEAT15 centroid distance over time (Å); dotted line: 62.7 Å in the B56γ holoenzyme (Day et al.). Same colours; amber is the 50 bp dsDNA loop.

points.text: Core RMSF 2.1–2.6 Å for apo, tet, clicked and ssDNA; only the N-tail (residues 1–13) moves 10+ Å

items.cap: Cβ7–Cβ553 against the clicked zero
Bare-strand restraint windows against the models

explain.text: <dfn>Cβ7–Cβ553</dfn>: the distance between the β-carbons of the two attachment residues, the coordinate the spring acts along (Å). Symbol: each system’s mean; thin line: its full range; bars: block SEM. <dfn>Δ</dfn> is the shift from the clicked protein without DNA (the right zero), with Welch’s p on ten block means.

x-axis: the spring’s end-to-end distance (Å); y-axis: force on the anchors (pN), + pushes them apart, − pulls them together. Lines are models: <dfn>Marko–Siggia</dfn> (worm-like chain: a single strand is an entropic spring that can only pull) and <dfn>Zocchi f(x)</dfn> (a bent duplex rod that pushes, and softens once it kinks). Points: forces measured on the bare strands held at 60 / 80 / 100 Å. Shading: where each chimera actually sits.

points.text: Against the clicked zero, ssDNA: −3.1 ± 3.5 Å (p = 0.39), not resolved
dsDNA: +34.4 ± 8.8 Å (p = 0.003): the sites are pushed apart, as the horseshoe unfolds
The strand sits at 95 Å, its own rms size: Marko–Siggia gives a 1.74 pN pull
Bare ss50 agrees with Marko–Siggia within error (−1.23 ± 1.70 pN at 100 Å)
Bare ds50 pushes +10 to +13 pN at 60–100 Å, about 13× Zocchi’s 0.9 pN
Answer: the duplex pushes far harder than modelled; a single strand pulls weakly and moves nothing measurable

items.cap: Bend, sharp turns, torsions and stacking along each strand
Strand size and modelled force over time

explain.text: Top row: 50 nt ssDNA; bottom row: the modified strand of the 50 bp dsDNA. Left: <dfn>bend</dfn> of the C4′ backbone trace at each nucleotide (°); pink bars (right axis): fraction of frames with a sharp > 90° turn, i.e. a <dfn>kink</dfn>. Middle: <dfn>BII fraction</dfn> (backbone torsion ε − ζ > 0, a sign of local strain) and how often a base is <dfn>unstacked</dfn> from its neighbour. Right: mean curvature against end-to-end distance; dotted lines: kink thresholds 2.6 (Zocchi), 5.5 (onset), 8.7 °/bp (certain).

Left: each strand’s end-to-end distance over time (Å, solid) and radius of gyration (dotted). Grey line: the rms size of a free 50-mer (94 Å); a single strand at that size is neither slack nor taut. Right: the force the models assign frame by frame (pN): Marko–Siggia pull for ssDNA, Zocchi push for dsDNA (drawn negative).

points.text: ssDNA end-to-end 95 ± 9 Å, right at its free rms size: neither slack nor taut
Sharp turns in 18 % of frames, hottest at nt 3 by the tether: no interior kink
78 % of adjacent bases stay stacked; 15 % of the backbone in BII
3 of 50 nt touch the protein at any time, mostly the N-tail (Met1–Asp5, Tet sites, Gln557)
dsDNA: 8.4°/bp with ≈ 36 base pairs open on average: the duplex melts rather than kinking cleanly
Answer: the strand is a relaxed coil that touches the protein; the dsDNA loop comes apart

items.title: cryoEM downstream analysis: how it differs from X-ray crystallography
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides; diffraction image and micrographs from the original slide (not PP2A data)

points.text: X-ray: the detector records only spot intensities, so the phases must be recovered (phasing) before any map exists
cryoEM: every particle image is a real-space projection with its phases intact, but the particle’s pose is unknown and its signal is buried in noise
CryoSPARC, TOPAZ: movies → 3D map. RELION, EMReady, COOT: map → atomic model
The next slides explain the boxed steps in order: defocus and the CTF, alignment, the Fourier slice theorem, reconstruction, classification and FSC

points.text: Stronger lens (shorter f): the rays cross before the sensor and spread into a disc

points.text: An amplitude object absorbs electrons: the wave leaves weaker, and the image is darker there
A phase object keeps the amplitude but delays the wave by φ (amplitude decrease is minor; the phase shift dominates)
A protein in ice is almost a pure phase object, and the detector records |ψ|² = |eiφ|² = 1: in focus it is nearly invisible

slides.title: Effect 2: the protein scatters the wave (diffraction)
slides.q: Where does each spatial frequency go?

items.title: Effect 2: the protein scatters the wave (diffraction)
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides

points.text: A repeat of spacing d scatters the wave by α ≈ λ/d (Bragg: 2d sin θ = λ, with α = 2θ)
Finer detail scatters further: the direction encodes the spatial frequency q = 1/d
The objective lens sends each direction to one point of its back focal plane: a Fourier transform of the object
At 300 kV (λ = 0.0197 Å) even 3 Å detail scatters by only ≈ 0.4°

slides.title: Key assumption: the weak phase object approximation
slides.q: Why is an in-focus protein invisible?

items.title: Key assumption: the weak phase object approximation
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides (φ exaggerated)

points.text: Exit wave Ψ<sub>exit</sub>(x, y) = e<sup>iφ(x,y)</sup>: the phasor turns by φ but keeps length 1
For |φ| ≪ 1: eiφ ≈ 1 + iφ = unscattered reference + scattered wave, 90° apart (i = eiπ/2)
Intensity |1 + iφ|² = 1 + φ² ≈ 1: no first-order contrast

slides.title: Key principle: defocus turns phase shifts into contrast
slides.q: How do we make the scattered wave visible?

items.title: Key principle: defocus turns phase shifts into contrast
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides (φ exaggerated)

points.text: Extra phase χ = π/2: the scattered wave becomes antiparallel to the reference, so the particle is dark
χ = 3π/2: parallel, so the particle is bright (contrast reversed)
Contrast ≈ −2φ sin χ: sin χ is the contrast transfer function, largest at χ = π/2 + kπ
Defocus supplies χ(q) = πλΔf q² − ½πC<sub>s</sub>λ³q⁴: a different extra phase for every spatial frequency q

slides.title: Each defocus value gives contrast to different spatial frequencies
slides.q: CTF(q) = sin χ(q), computed for 300 kV and Cₛ = 2.7 mm

items.title: Each defocus value gives contrast to different spatial frequencies
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides; CTF computed live

points.text: Zeros: the image carries no information at those q. Negative lobes: contrast reversed
More defocus: stronger low-resolution contrast and faster oscillation. Thon rings reveal each micrograph’s Δf (CTF estimation)
Collecting over a range of Δf puts the zeros at different q, so every q is measured somewhere
An envelope also damps high q: high resolution needs many averaged particles

slides.title: Forward model: what one particle image contains
slides.q: How do projection, the CTF and noise alter an observation?

items.cap: Ian’s Manim clip 01: mathematical illustration in dimensionless units (each click plays the next beat)

points.text: Projection: the beam integrates the 3D potential along z, so one view cannot fix depth
CTF: every spatial frequency is scaled, removed (at a zero) or sign-reversed (negative lobe)
Noise: independent and comparable to the signal here; far larger than it in real micrographs
Together, in Fourier space:Yi(q) = Ci(q) Ṽ(Riᵀ[qx, qy, 0]ᵀ) e−2πi q·ti + Ni(q)
Known: the image Yi and its CTF Ci (from the fitted Δf). Unknown: each particle’s pose (Ri, ti) and the 3D potential V
Two Fourier rules keep it simple: a shift becomes a phase ramp e−2πi q·t, and a blur (convolution) becomes a product, so the CTF just multiplies
Ultimate goal: the 3D potential V in real space, to fit the atomic model into

slides.title: 2D classification: align first, then average
slides.q: Why align before averaging, and how fast does the noise fall?

items.cap: Ian’s Manim clip 02: mathematical illustration in dimensionless units (each click plays the next beat)

points.text: Every image is the same pattern, rotated by φi and shifted by ti, plus noise
Averaging without aligning smears the dots into rings
Undo each rotation and shift first: the average is sharp, and only noise is left in the residual
Noise falls as σ/√N: 4× more particles give 2× the signal-to-noise ratio
2D classification does this for groups of similar views at once; junk particles collect in junk classes and are discarded

slides.title: Central slice theorem: every image is a plane through the 3D Fourier transform
slides.q: How do unknown 3D orientations and Fourier slices define reconstruction?

items.cap: Ian’s Manim clip 03: mathematical illustration in dimensionless units (each click plays the next beat)

points.text: Orientation R: a viewing direction (2 angles) plus an in-plane rotation ψ (1 angle) = 3 degrees of freedom
Projection(PRV)(x, y) = ∫ V(Rᵀ(x, y, z)ᵀ) dzChanging R changes the beam direction; sliding a dot along the beam leaves the image unchanged
Fourier slice theoremℱ₂{PRV}(q) = V̂(Rᵀ(qx, qy, 0)ᵀ)The 2D transform of an image is the central plane of the 3D transform, perpendicular to the beam
Why: integrating over z and then transforming in x, y is the same as the 3D transform evaluated at k<sub>z</sub> = 0
Coverage: well-spread views sample 92 % of the Fourier ball; views within 15° of one axis sample 26 % and leave a missing cone
With known poses, inserting slices and inverting converges on the true structure as views are added
In practice the poses are unknown: the density and every pose must be estimated together

slides.title: Reconstruction scheme 1: you know the poses
slides.q: Least squares: L(v) = ½ Σᵢ (yᵢ − Aᵢv)ᵀ Σᵢ⁻¹ (yᵢ − Aᵢv); ∇L = 0 gives the normal equations

items.title: Reconstruction scheme 1: you know the poses
items.cap: Live 2D reconstruction (64 × 64, nearest-neighbour gridding, noisy images) computed in the browser

points.text: One image = one central line (a plane in 3D). Backprojecting it gives only streaks
More views fan out from the origin: low frequencies are measured by every image, high ones by few
The backprojection (right-hand side) over-counts the centre, so it is blurred; dividing by the count (left-hand matrix) sharpens it
Noise averages down where a frequency is measured often; the edges stay noisy (hence weighting and regularisation)
Preferred orientation leaves a missing wedge (a cone in 3D) that no amount of averaging fills

slides.title: Reconstruction scheme 2: you don’t know any poses
slides.q: What does iterative reconstruction optimise?

items.cap: Ian’s Manim clip 04: mathematical illustration in dimensionless units (each click plays the next beat)

points.text: Compare each image with the projection predicted from the current map; the residual measures the mismatch
Pose step: hold the map and search each particle’s orientation and shift to shrink its residual
Map step: hold the poses and update the map (scheme 1). Alternate until the loss stops falling; one particle here stays in a local minimum

Ab initio (no starting map): CryoSPARC combines branch-and-bound pose search with stochastic gradient descent on random mini-batches ℬ:V(t+1) = V(t) − ηt (1/|ℬ|) Σi∈ℬ ∇V ℓi(V(t))Cheap, noisy steps; no guarantee of the global optimum
Regularisation: a smaller data misfit is not a better map; without a penalty the fit chases the noise
Risk: aligning noisy images to a reference that already contains the same noise reinforces it. The defence is two independent half-sets (FSC, two slides on)

slides.title: Heterogeneity: classification separates conformations
slides.q: How do heterogeneity and classification interact?

items.cap: Ian’s Manim clip 05: mathematical illustration in dimensionless units (each click plays the next beat)

points.text: Two states that differ in one dot (state A vs state B)
Averaging a mixed set blurs the moving part: dot 5 appears faintly in both places
PCA: each image becomes a point; PC1 separates the states, PC2 is noise
A two-class Gaussian mixture fit by EM gives each image a probability for each class (soft assignment)
Class averages recover both states. In CryoSPARC, 3D classification and heterogeneous refinement do this with 3D maps

slides.title: Half-maps and FSC: how resolution is judged
slides.q: Which resolution measures exist, and why keep them apart?

items.cap: Ian’s Manim clip 06: mathematical illustration in dimensionless units (each click plays the next beat)

points.text: Split the particles into two halves and refine each independently: the signal agrees, the noise does not
Fourier shell correlation, shell by shell (Sq = all k with |k| ≈ q):FSC(q) = Σ V̂A(k) V̂B(k)* / √(Σ |V̂A|² Σ |V̂B|²)
Resolution d = 1/q where the half-map FSC falls below 0.143 (the gold-standard criterion)
One global number hides variation: local resolution is worse in flexible regions
Map–model FSC (cutoff 0.5) checks the fitted atomic model against the map
Neither cutoff is a positional error bar or a physical limit
